claim: Dengue viruses cause clinical disease in approximately 100 million individuals each year.
source: Dengue viruses cause clinical disease in approximately 100 million individuals each year and are found in over 100 countries (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013

claim: Dengue viruses are found in over 100 countries.
source: Dengue viruses cause clinical disease in approximately 100 million individuals each year and are found in over 100 countries (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013

claim: No vaccine exists that conveys cross-protection against all human dengue viruses.
source: Yet, to date no vaccine exists that conveys cross-protection against all human dengue viruses (Scherwitzl et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scherwitzl et al., 2017

claim: Dengue viruses are positive sense RNA viruses in the family Flaviviridae.
source: Dengue viruses are positive sense RNA viruses in the family Flaviviridae, and are related to yellow fever virus, Zika virus, and West Nile virus (Best, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Best, 2016

claim: Dengue viruses are related to yellow fever virus, Zika virus, and West Nile virus.
source: Dengue viruses are positive sense RNA viruses in the family Flaviviridae, and are related to yellow fever virus, Zika virus, and West Nile virus (Best, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Best, 2016

claim: Dengue viruses are primarily transmitted between humans in highly populated areas by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes.
source: These viruses are primarily transmitted between humans in highly populated areas by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, in what are referred to as human (or 'urban') transmission cycles (Diamond and Pierson, 2015; Hanley et al., 2013; Vasilakis et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Diamond and Pierson, 2015; Hanley et al., 2013; Vasilakis et al., 2011

claim: Sylvatic dengue virus transmission cycles exist in Asia and Africa and involve nonhuman primates and forest-dwelling Aedes mosquitos.
source: Sylvatic (i.e. forest) dengue virus transmission cycles, which are separate from the human transmission cycles, exist in Asia and Africa and involve nonhuman primates and forest-dwelling Aedes mosquitos (Vasilakis et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2000; Rico-Hesse, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vasilakis et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2000; Rico-Hesse, 1990

claim: The exact nonhuman primate species that serve as the sustaining natural reservoirs for sylvatic dengue viruses are unknown.
source: While the exact nonhuman primate species that serve as the sustaining natural reservoirs for sylvatic dengue viruses are unknown, the global distribution of both dengue viruses and their transmitting mosquitoes could be consistent with a significant number of primate species being involved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Hanley et al., 2013; Vasilakis et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanley et al., 2013; Vasilakis et al., 2011

claim: Human dengue viruses cluster into four phylogenetically distinct clades referred to as DENV1, 2, 3, and 4.
source: Human dengue viruses cluster into four phylogenetically distinct clades referred to as DENV1, 2, 3, and 4 (Vasilakis and Weaver, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vasilakis and Weaver, 2008

claim: These clades have sylvatic dengue virus isolates at their bases, supporting zoonotic origins of the four dengue viruses that now circulate in humans.
source: These clades have sylvatic dengue virus isolates at their bases, supporting zoonotic origins of the four dengue viruses that now circulate in humans (Wang et al., 2000; Pyke et al., 2016; Weaver and Vasilakis, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000; Pyke et al., 2016; Weaver and Vasilakis, 2009

claim: Human dengue viruses have now become uncoupled from the sylvatic reservoir and require only humans and mosquitoes to be sustained.
source: Human dengue viruses have now become uncoupled from the sylvatic reservoir and require only humans and mosquitoes to be sustained (Mayer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayer et al., 2017

claim: In side-by-side experiments, sylvatic and human dengue viruses replicate similarly in human cells.
source: In side-by-side experiments, sylvatic and human dengue viruses replicate similarly in human cells (Vasilakis et al., 2007; Vasilakis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vasilakis et al., 2007; Vasilakis et al., 2008

claim: Dengue does not replicate to high titers in chimpanzees.
source: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) (Scherer et al., 1978), rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) (Halstead et al., 1973; Hickey et al., 2013), marmosets (multiple Callithrix species) (Moi et al., 2013; Ferreira et al., 2014), and other nonhuman primate species (Althouse et al., 2014) have been explored as possible primate models for studying dengue virus pathogenesis and for vaccine challenge. In general, it has been observed that dengue does not replicate to high titers in these models, and little or no overt disease pathology is observed (Cassetti et al., 2010; Zompi and Harris, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scherer et al., 1978; Cassetti et al., 2010; Zompi and Harris, 2012

claim: Dengue does not replicate to high titers in rhesus macaques.
source: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) (Scherer et al., 1978), rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) (Halstead et al., 1973; Hickey et al., 2013), marmosets (multiple Callithrix species) (Moi et al., 2013; Ferreira et al., 2014), and other nonhuman primate species (Althouse et al., 2014) have been explored as possible primate models for studying dengue virus pathogenesis and for vaccine challenge. In general, it has been observed that dengue does not replicate to high titers in these models, and little or no overt disease pathology is observed (Cassetti et al., 2010; Zompi and Harris, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Halstead et al., 1973; Hickey et al., 2013; Cassetti et al., 2010; Zompi and Harris, 2012

source: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) (Scherer et al., 1978), rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) (Halstead et al., 1973; Hickey et al., 2013), marmosets (multiple Callithrix species) (Moi et al., 2013; Ferreira et al., 2014), and other nonhuman primate species (Althouse et al., 2014) have been explored as possible primate models for studying dengue virus pathogenesis and for vaccine challenge. claim: STING is a multi-pass transmembrane protein found in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: STING is a multi-pass transmembrane protein found in the endoplasmic reticulum, and functions as a critical component in the innate immune sensing pathway for intracellular pathogens (Ishikawa and Barber, 2008; Zhong et al., 2008; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2009; Burdette and Vance, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ishikawa and Barber, 2008; Zhong et al., 2008; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2009; Burdette and Vance, 2013

claim: STING functions as a critical component in the innate immune sensing pathway for intracellular pathogens.
source: STING is a multi-pass transmembrane protein found in the endoplasmic reticulum, and functions as a critical component in the innate immune sensing pathway for intracellular pathogens (Ishikawa and Barber, 2008; Zhong et al., 2008; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2009; Burdette and Vance, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ishikawa and Barber, 2008; Zhong et al., 2008; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2009; Burdette and Vance, 2013

claim: STING was originally described as part of the response to cytosolic DNA sensing.
source: Although originally described as part of the response to cytosolic DNA sensing (Zhang et al., 2011), STING is also activated upon RNA virus infection (Holm et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011

claim: STING is also activated upon RNA virus infection.
source: Although originally described as part of the response to cytosolic DNA sensing (Zhang et al., 2011), STING is also activated upon RNA virus infection (Holm et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holm et al., 2016

claim: Several RNA viruses encode proteins that antagonize or degrade STING.
source: Underscoring this, several RNA viruses encode proteins that antagonize or degrade STING (Sun et al., 2012; Nitta et al., 2013; Ding et al., 2013; Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2012; Nitta et al., 2013; Ding et al., 2013; Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012

claim: The NS2B3 protease of DENV2 has been shown to target human STING for cleavage.
source: For instance, the NS2B3 protease of one human dengue virus, DENV2, has been shown to target human STING for cleavage (Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012

claim: Through the cleavage of STING, DENV2 renders the host unable to induce the phosphorylation of Interferon Regulatory Factor 3 (IRF3), therefore decreasing production of type I interferon and increasing viral titers.
source: Through the cleavage of STING, DENV2 renders the host unable to induce the phosphorylation of Interferon Regulatory Factor 3 (IRF3), therefore decreasing production of type I interferon and increasing viral titers (Green et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Green et al., 2014

claim: Mouse STING is resistant to cleavage by the DENV2 protease.
source: Mouse STING is resistant to cleavage by the DENV2 protease (Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012

claim: Mice mount an effective immune response against dengue viruses, protecting them against infection and compromising their utility as model organisms.
source: This at least partially explains why mice mount an effective immune response against dengue viruses, protecting them against infection and compromising their utility as model organisms (Cassetti et al., 2010; Zompi and Harris, 2012; Ashour et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cassetti et al., 2010; Zompi and Harris, 2012; Ashour et al., 2010

claim: The NS2B3 proteases of human (DENV1-4) and sylvatic dengue viruses universally cleave human STING.
source: In this study, we show that the NS2B3 proteases of human (DENV1-4) and sylvatic dengue viruses universally cleave human STING.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: None of the dengue virus proteases can cleave the STING proteins of chimpanzees, macaques, or marmosets.
source: However, none of these proteases can cleave the STING proteins of chimpanzees, macaques, or marmosets, three primate species that have been pursued as model organisms.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: An 'RG' motif at positions 78/79 of STING is critical for susceptibility to cleavage.
source: We show that an 'RG' motif at positions 78/79 of STING is critical for susceptibility to cleavage, and conversion of these residues to 'RG' renders all nonhuman primate STING proteins tested, as well as mouse STING, sensitive to dengue virus proteases.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Conversion of residues 78/79 to 'RG' renders all nonhuman primate STING proteins tested sensitive to dengue virus proteases.
source: We show that an 'RG' motif at positions 78/79 of STING is critical for susceptibility to cleavage, and conversion of these residues to 'RG' renders all nonhuman primate STING proteins tested, as well as mouse STING, sensitive to dengue virus proteases.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Conversion of residues 78/79 to 'RG' renders mouse STING sensitive to dengue virus proteases.
source: We show that an 'RG' motif at positions 78/79 of STING is critical for susceptibility to cleavage, and conversion of these residues to 'RG' renders all nonhuman primate STING proteins tested, as well as mouse STING, sensitive to dengue virus proteases.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The DENV2 protease cannot cleave chimpanzee STING.
source: Remarkably, the DENV2 protease could not even cleave chimpanzee STING, which differs from human STING at only three amino acid positions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Chimpanzee STING differs from human STING at only three amino acid positions.
source: Remarkably, the DENV2 protease could not even cleave chimpanzee STING, which differs from human STING at only three amino acid positions.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data presented in the manuscript

claim: The dengue virus cleavage site in STING was previously mapped to between the 95th and 96th residues.
source: The dengue virus cleavage site in STING was previously mapped to between the 95th and 96th residues (Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012

claim: Human and chimpanzee STING differ at only three amino acid positions, residues 78, 230, and 232.
source: Human and chimpanzee STING differ at only three amino acid positions, residues 78, 230, and 232.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data presented in the manuscript

claim: Mutating the human STING to encode the chimpanzee residue at site 78 (78W) caused it to become resistant to cleavage by DENV NS2B3.
source: We found that mutating the human STING to encode the chimpanzee residue at site 78 (78W) caused it to become resistant to cleavage by DENV NS2B3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mutating the chimpanzee STING at residue 78 to the human amino acid (78R) rendered the chimpanzee STING susceptible to cleavage.
source: Likewise, mutating the chimpanzee STING at residue 78 to the human amino acid (78R) rendered the chimpanzee STING susceptible to cleavage (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mutations at site 230 had no effect on STING cleavage, either alone or in combination with residue 78.
source: We saw no effect of mutations at a second site, 230, either alone or in combination with residue 78 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: STING site 78 may be important for retention in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Previously, it had been shown that STING site 78 may be important for retention in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Sun et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2009

claim: Both wildtype and 78W mutant human STING similarly localized to the ER.
source: Both the wildtype and mutant STING similarly localized to the ER (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Position 78R is a critical determinant for dengue virus cleavage, either as a binding site or a cleavage site for the dengue protease.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that position 78R is a critical determinant for dengue virus cleavage, either as a binding site or a cleavage site for the dengue protease.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that mutations at position 78 affect cleavage susceptibility

claim: STING is cleaved in a way that divides the protein into approximately 25% and 75% of its original molecular weight, with the N-terminus of the protein representing the smaller portion.
source: It was previously estimated that STING is cleaved in a way that divides the protein into approximately 25% and 75% of its original molecular weight, with the N-terminus of the protein representing the smaller portion (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2012

claim: The 78/79 'RG' motif is in good agreement with what is known about the preferences of NS2B3, where glycine (G) often lies directly downstream of the peptide cleavage site, and an arginine (R) directly upstream.
source: In addition, the 78/79 'RG' motif is in good agreement with what is known about the preferences of NS2B3, where glycine (G) often lies directly downstream of the peptide cleavage site, and an arginine (R) directly upstream (Li et al., 2005a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005a

claim: pIRF3 was reduced when human or chimpanzee STING was susceptible to NS2B3 cleavage.
source: We found that pIRF3 was reduced when human or chimpanzee STING was susceptible to NS2B3 cleavage, and not reduced when STING was resistant to cleavage (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C

claim: pIRF3 was not reduced when STING was resistant to cleavage.
source: We found that pIRF3 was reduced when human or chimpanzee STING was susceptible to NS2B3 cleavage, and not reduced when STING was resistant to cleavage (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C

claim: With human STING and the version of chimpanzee STING rendered sensitive to cleavage (78R), there was a significant reduction in firefly luciferase production in the presence of active NS2B3, in comparison to the catalytically dead version of the protease.
source: With human STING and the version of chimpanzee STING rendered sensitive to cleavage (78R), there was a significant reduction in firefly luciferase production in the presence of active NS2B3, in comparison to the catalytically dead version of the protease (Figure 2C, top).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: This reduction in luciferase is not observed with chimpanzee STING, or with human STING rendered resistant to cleavage by the 78W mutation.
source: This reduction is not observed with chimpanzee STING, or with human STING rendered resistant to cleavage by the 78W mutation.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: A549 cells re-complemented with STING, regardless of the version, produced less dengue virus than the STING knockout cell line that was not re-complemented.
source: We found that A549 cells re-complemented with STING, regardless of the version, produced less dengue virus than the STING knockout cell line that was not re-complemented (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by viral titration data shown in Figure 3

claim: Cells re-complemented with a cleavage-resistant STING produced less virus than those re-complemented with a cleavage-susceptible STING.
source: However, cells re-complemented with a cleavage-resistant STING produced less virus than those re-complemented with a cleavage-susceptible STING (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by viral titration data shown in Figure 3

claim: Cell lines that differ by only a single amino acid in STING demonstrate as much as a 176-fold change in infectious virus produced at 24 hr post-infection.
source: In fact, cell lines in this experiment that differ by only a single amino acid in STING demonstrate as much as a 176-fold change in infectious virus produced at 24 hr post-infection, according to the titration experiments (human versus human 78W STING).
evidence: Supported by viral titration data shown in Figure 3

claim: Cleavage of STING is critically important for dengue virus replication, and has a large impact on viral titers.
source: This suggests that cleavage of STING is critically important for dengue virus replication, and has a large impact on viral titers.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing large differences in viral titers based on STING cleavage susceptibility

claim: The dengue protease also cannot cleave rhesus macaque, marmoset, or mouse STING.
source: The dengue protease also cannot cleave rhesus macaque, marmoset, or mouse STING (Figure 1B), all of which deviate from the 'RG' motif found in human STING (highlighted green in Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Rhesus macaque, marmoset, and mouse STING all deviate from the 'RG' motif found in human STING.
source: The dengue protease also cannot cleave rhesus macaque, marmoset, or mouse STING (Figure 1B), all of which deviate from the 'RG' motif found in human STING (highlighted green in Figure 4A).

claim: Mutations that restored the 'RG' motif to rhesus macaque, marmoset, and mouse STING restored susceptibility to cleavage.
source: We found that, in all cases, mutations that restored this motif to the human 'RG' restored susceptibility to cleavage (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Mutation of residues 93–96 in mouse STING to match the human 'LRRG' did not confer susceptibility to cleavage by NS2B3.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012), mutation of residues 93–96 in mouse STING to match the human 'LRRG' did not confer susceptibility to cleavage by NS2B3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and citations to Aguirre et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2012

claim: Sites 78 and 79 are critical determinants for cleavage by the DENV NS2B3 protease.
source: Overall, these results further support the conclusion that sites 78 and 79 are critical determinants for cleavage by the DENV NS2B3 protease.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing that mutations at these sites affect cleavage susceptibility

claim: An 'RG' motif at positions 78/79 is both necessary and sufficient to make primate and rodent STING susceptible to cleavage by the DENV2 protease.
source: An 'RG' motif at these two positions is both necessary and sufficient to make primate and rodent STING susceptible to cleavage by the DENV2 protease.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that the RG motif determines cleavage susceptibility across multiple species

claim: All proteases from DENV1-4 were able to cleave wildtype human STING far more efficiently than human STING bearing the 78W mutation.
source: While some of these proteases expressed better than others, all were able to cleave wildtype human STING far more efficiently than human STING bearing the 78W mutation (Figure 5A).

claim: The 78/79 RG motif of STING is recognized (i.e. bound or cleaved) by the NS2B3 proteases of all endemic human dengue viruses.
source: This data indicates that the 78/79 RG motif of STING is recognized (i.e. bound or cleaved) by the NS2B3 proteases of all endemic human dengue viruses.

claim: The proteases of all four endemic human dengue viruses have similar cleavage motif preferences.
source: If residues 78/79 in fact constitute the actual cleavage site for the protease, this would be in line with biochemical studies showing that the proteases of all four endemic human dengue viruses have similar cleavage motif preferences (Li et al., 2005a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005a

claim: The sylvatic dengue virus protease (DakAr-141069) cleaves human STING.
source: We find that this viral protease also cleaves human STING, but not the STING of chimpanzee, rhesus macaque, or marmoset (Figure 5B).

claim: The sylvatic dengue virus protease (DakAr-141069) does not cleave the STING of chimpanzee, rhesus macaque, or marmoset.
source: We find that this viral protease also cleaves human STING, but not the STING of chimpanzee, rhesus macaque, or marmoset (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The restoration of the 'RG' motif at positions 78/79 renders chimpanzee, rhesus macaque, and marmoset STING proteins susceptible to cleavage by the sylvatic protease.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The sylvatic protease is targeting (i.e. binding or cleaving) the same cleavage determinant as the proteases from human dengue viruses.
source: Further, the restoration of the 'RG' motif at positions 78/79 again renders all of these STING proteins susceptible to cleavage (Figure 5B), indicating that the sylvatic protease is targeting (i.e. binding or cleaving) the same cleavage determinant as the proteases from human dengue viruses.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that the same mutations affect cleavage by both sylvatic and human dengue proteases

claim: With the exception of chimpanzees and bonobos, all apes encode the same amino acids as human in the 78/79 motif, constituting the correct cleavage determinant for dengue virus.
source: With the exception of chimpanzees and bonobos, all apes encode the same amino acids as human in this motif, constituting the correct cleavage determinant for dengue virus.

claim: No monkey species encodes an 'RG' at positions 78/79.
source: In contrast, no monkey species encodes an 'RG' at positions 78/79.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Old World monkeys all encode 'RD' at positions 78/79.

evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6A

claim: New World monkeys encode a 'QG' at positions 78/79.
source: Also, no monkeys from the Americas encode an 'RG' at these residues, and instead these species encode a 'QG' at positions 78/79, just like the marmoset clone tested herein.

claim: Mice and pigs do not have the correct RG residues at STING 78/79.
source: Mice and pigs, two current models for dengue virus infection (Cassetti et al., 2010), also do not have the correct RG residues at STING 78/79 (Figure 6A).

claim: Out of the entire Genbank database, only two other mammals were identified that share the exact same sequence as humans in the eight amino acid region surrounding the newly identified dengue virus cleavage determinant in STING: chinchilla and naked mole rat.
source: Out of the entire database, only two other mammals were identified that share the exact same sequence as humans in the eight amino acid region surrounding the newly identified dengue virus cleavage determinant in STING: chinchilla and naked mole rat, both of which are rodents (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The desert woodrat has the RG at positions 78/79, but encodes two amino acid substitutions just downstream of these residues, compared to human STING.
source: A third rodent species, the desert woodrat, has the RG at positions 78/79, but encodes two amino acid substitutions just downstream of these residues, compared to human STING (Figure 6A).

claim: The STING of naked mole rat and desert woodrat is clearly cleaved by the DENV2 protease.
source: We see that the STING of naked mole rat and desert woodrat is clearly cleaved by the DENV2 protease, in that the cleavage product is evident (Figure 6B).

claim: The STING band for chinchilla disappears in the presence of active protease, but no cleavage product is detected.

claim: In humans cells, sylvatic and human dengue viruses replicate similarly.

claim: There are critical differences between human and monkey hosts in terms of dengue virus replication.

claim: All dengue viruses cleave human STING, but not the versions of STING found in most other mammals.

claim: Only some apes and three rodent species, out of all of the mammalian STING sequences in Genbank, encode an RG at positions 78/79.

evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Dengue viruses have achieved increased titers in humans by evolving to recognize a portion of human STING that is not conserved in the STING of the wild and more rare animals that serve as their sustaining reservoir in nature.
source: Remarkably, though, dengue viruses have achieved this by evolving to recognize a portion of human STING that is not conserved in the STING of the wild and more rare animals that serve as their sustaining reservoir in nature, allowing the viruses to maintain decreased pathogenicity in these species.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: The evolution of the viral proteases to cleave human STING and simultaneously to avoid cleavage of monkey STING would be expected to reduce virus titers in monkeys.
source: The evolution of the viral proteases to cleave human STING and simultaneously to avoid cleavage of monkey STING would be expected to reduce virus titers in monkeys, as the interferon pathway would be at least partially enabled.

claim: Sylvatic dengue viruses have been isolated directly from macaques (Macaca fascicularis) and leaf monkeys (Presbytis obscura) that were placed as sentinels in forest canopies.

claim: Most sylvatic dengue viruses have been obtained from forest mosquitoes or from humans that contracted the virus in the forest.
